**On Pencil Stubs**

There is a drawer in nearly every home that holds pencil stubs too short to sharpen comfortably, yet too dignified to throw away. These little artifacts deserve more respect than they receive. A pencil stub is a biography in graphite and wood—six inches of potential whittled down by grocery lists, crossword puzzles, phone numbers scrawled in kitchens before cell phones memorized everything for us.

Consider what the stub has survived: the first-day-of-school nerves of some child, now middle-aged; the doodles drawn during a boring meeting; the love letter abandoned halfway through because typing felt easier. Somewhere along the way, its eraser wore down to a metal band, meaning every mistake it recorded stayed recorded—or was smudged away with a fingertip, which is its own kind of tenderness.

We live in an era of infinite undo, and there's something to be said for instruments that don't offer it. A pencil at least lets you erase, but imperfectly. The ghost of the wrong word remains, pressed into the page's fibers. This seems honest. Most corrections in life work this way—the error leaves a residue even after it's fixed.

So keep your stubs. Let them rattle around the drawer with dead batteries and rubber bands. One day you'll need to mark something quickly, and you'll fish one out, feel its familiar heft, and be briefly, wordlessly connected to every hand that ever held it down to nothing. That's not trash. That's lineage, worn smooth by use.
